title: Here comes the sun (Sonne)
summary: Rammstein's boxing-ring song: count from one to ten with the whole world, and learn why the sun is 'she' and yet 'der hellste Stern'.
goals: Count one to ten at full speed, the way the song does
Understand the chorus: Hier kommt die Sonne
Hear the boxing match hidden in the lyrics
See how gender follows the noun: die Sonne, der Stern

sections.title: About this song
sections.text:
**Rammstein** are a metal band from Berlin, famous far beyond Germany. 'Sonne' was the first single from their album **Mutter**, released on 12 February 2001, and it reached number 2 in Germany.

The song was first written as a ring entrance song for the Ukrainian boxer **Vitali Klitschko**, who never used it. Once you know that, the lyrics are a boxing match: the count, the fists, the fighter going down. In the video the band are the seven dwarfs, mining gold for Snow White.

Why it's good for you: the chorus is the numbers from Unit 0, shouted one by one, and the other lines are short and clear.

items.de: Eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, aus!
items.en: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, out!
items.note: In boxing the referee counts to ten; at 'aus' the fighter is out.

sections.title: Counting like a referee
sections.text:
- The song counts where the boxing referee counts: [[aus]] means **out**, as in knocked out. You know [[aus]] as 'from' ([[Ich komme aus Armenien.]]); here it's the other meaning, 'over, finished': [[Das Licht ist aus.]] (The light is off.)
- In the chorus each line starts with the next number: (Eins) ... (Zwei) ... up to (Acht, neun). Say the numbers along with the song: it's the fastest number drill you'll get.
- Listen to the R: Till Lindemann rolls it hard and long, like a very strong Russian р or Armenian ռ. That exaggerated roll is his stage style. Textbook German uses a throat r, and many people in Bavaria roll it lightly (Unit 0), so your own r is fine.

items.en: Everyone is waiting for the light
Be afraid, do not be afraid
items.note: sich fürchten = to be afraid; a command to several people (ihr)

sections.title: What's going on
sections.text:
- [[Alle warten auf das Licht]]: [[warten auf]] is 'wait **for**', with auf, not 'für'. You'll say it at every bus stop: [[Ich warte auf den Bus.]] [[alle]] = everyone (all of them).
- [[Fürchtet euch nicht]] is a famous phrase: in Luther's German Bible, it's what the angel says in the Christmas story (Lukas 2,10), 'Fear not'. Rammstein play with it: first 'be afraid', then 'don't be afraid'.
- [[fürchtet euch]] is a command to a group ([[ihr]]), and [[sich fürchten]] (to be afraid) takes a 'self' word: [[ich fürchte mich]], [[ihr fürchtet euch]]. Commands come in Unit 5; for now, notice the pattern.

sections.title: The sun shines out of me

items.de: Die Sonne scheint mir aus den Augen
items.en: The sun shines out of my eyes
items.note: mir = to me; here it means 'my' eyes

items.de: Sie wird heut Nacht nicht untergeh'n
items.note: heut = heute; untergeh'n = untergehen (to set, of the sun)

items.de: Und die Welt zählt laut bis zehn
items.en: And the world counts out loud to ten

sections.title: Grammar in the lines
sections.text:
- [[scheint mir aus den Augen]]: German often says whose body part it is with [[mir]] (to me), not with 'my': [[Mir tut der Kopf weh.]] (My head hurts: Unit 6.) So 'the sun shines to me out of the eyes' = out of **my** eyes.
- [[Sie wird ... nicht untergehen]]: [[werden]] + verb at the end = the future ('will'). [[untergehen]] is what the sun does in the evening: [[Die Sonne geht unter.]] (The sun is setting.) It's a separable verb: Unit 3.
- [[heut]] and [[untergeh'n]]: song German drops letters to fit the rhythm, like [[ich sitz]] in 'Barfuß am Klavier'. Written: [[heute]], [[untergehen]].
- [[Die Welt zählt laut bis zehn]]: the whole world is the referee counting. [[laut]] = loud, out loud.

items.note: verb in second place, after hier

items.de: Sie ist der hellste Stern von allen
items.en: She is the brightest star of all
items.note: hell = bright; der hellste = the brightest

sections.title: She, but der Stern
sections.text:
[[Sie ist der hellste Stern]]: the sun is [[die Sonne]], so it's [[sie]] (she). But [[der Stern]] is masculine, so 'the brightest star' is [[der hellste Stern]]. Each noun keeps its own gender, whatever it describes.

Russian swaps these two: солнце is neuter and луна feminine, while German has **die** Sonne and **der** Mond (the moon). Don't copy the Russian gender here: the sun is a she in German, the moon a he.

items.de: Lässt dich hart zu Boden geh'n
items.en: Sends you hard to the floor
items.note: zu Boden gehen = to go down (in boxing); lassen = to let, to make

sections.title: How to use it
sections.text:
1. Watch the video once with the link above, just for fun.
2. Play it again and count along with the chorus, out loud: eins, zwei, drei ... Try to keep up.
3. Shout [[Hier kommt die Sonne]] with the band. Loud is fine, it's Rammstein.
4. Close the video and count from one to ten as fast as you can, then backwards from zehn.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: Here comes the sun.
items.explanation: kommen, er/sie/es kommt. The verb comes second, right after hier.

items.question: At the end of the count, 'aus' means out, over. Which sentence uses 'aus' the same way?
items.explanation: Das Licht ist aus = the light is off (over, out). In the other two, aus means 'from'.

items.question: The sun is 'die Sonne'. Which sentence is correct?
items.explanation: der Stern is masculine, so der hellste Stern, even when it describes die Sonne. Each noun keeps its own gender.

items.audio: Und die Welt zählt laut bis zehn
items.question: Up to which number does the world count?
items.explanation: bis zehn = up to ten, the full boxing count.
